issue.title: Native seatbelt-style ratchet for bulk suppressions

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

issue.body:
Hi!
Would you consider building an eslint-seatbelt equivalent into oxlint natively, as a ratchet mode for bulk suppressions? Existing errors would be allowed per file and rule, counts could only go down unless you allow an increase on purpose, and the baseline would tighten itself as people fix things.

We recently switched Expensify/App from ESLint to oxlint as our blocking linter ([Expensify/App#105376](https://github.com/Expensify/App/pull/105376)). Before the switch we used [eslint-seatbelt](https://github.com/justjake/eslint-seatbelt) to grandfather existing violations, and we didn't want to lose that, so we rewrote it as a small post-processor that runs on oxlint's output ([Seatbelt.ts](https://github.com/Expensify/App/blob/4ea5116169f223d870782ebd793394d71b9c1764/scripts/lint/processors/Seatbelt.ts)).

It works well for us, but we'd love to see something like it built into oxlint natively. We're trying to drop ESLint entirely and run as much as we can on plain oxlint, and from the [RFC](https://github.com/oxc-project/oxc/discussions/22198) thread it looks like a lot of teams are writing this same wrapper. It also isn't more rules for you to support, since it sits on top of the bulk suppressions you already shipped.

### How we use it

Every rule in our config is an error. Existing violations live in a baseline file ([oxlint.seatbelt.tsv](https://github.com/Expensify/App/blob/4ea5116169f223d870782ebd793394d71b9c1764/config/oxlint/oxlint.seatbelt.tsv)) with a count per file and rule. This is what lets us turn on something strict straight away, without leaving it at `warn` for months.

The baseline works as a ratchet:

| What happened | Locally | PR CI | `main` CI |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Count unchanged | Pass | Pass | Nothing |
| Count went down | Pass, file untouched | Pass | Bot commits the lower count |
| Count went up | Fail | Fail | Fail |
| Count went up with `SEATBELT_INCREASE=<rule>` | Pass, you commit the TSV change | Pass | n/a |

Fixing an old error never fails the build and never makes you regenerate the baseline. CI tightens it after merge. With this many open PRs, making everyone commit baseline changes would mean constant conflicts on one file.

Expensify/App is open source. The contributor docs are in [LINTING.md](https://github.com/Expensify/App/blob/4ea5116169f223d870782ebd793394d71b9c1764/contributingGuides/LINTING.md#L43-L63) and implementation details are in [scripts/lint](https://github.com/Expensify/App/tree/4ea5116169f223d870782ebd793394d71b9c1764/scripts/lint).

Thanks for considering it, and for all the work on oxlint so far!

comment.body: Hi, thanks for the interest and feedback on this feature. We are actively making progress on this feature and are planning to complete it this quarter (see https://github.com/oxc-project/oxc/issues/28275). We are supporting an ESLint-style bulk suppressions scheme for compatibility/familiarity and this is actually [already shipped in the CLI](github.com/oxc-project/oxc/pull/19328), but it is currently undocumented (hidden flags) while we work on stabilizing Language Server Protocol support and finish testing it. Please feel free to give it a try and give us feedback!

linter: typescript/no-use-before-define doesn't have parity with @typescript-eslint/no-use-before-define
linter: no-use-before-define flags instance fields with classes: false
issue.body:
### What version of Oxlint are you using?

1.90.0

### What command did you run?

```sh
oxlint --config .oxlintrc.json --max-warnings 0 example.ts
```

### What does your `.oxlintrc.json` config file look like?

```json
{
  "rules": {
    "no-use-before-define": [
      "warn",
      { "functions": false, "classes": false, "variables": false }
    ]
  }
}
```

### Minimal reproduction

```ts
export class Parent {
  child = new Child();
}

class Child {}
```

### What happened?

Oxlint reports the reference in the instance field initializer:

```text
example.ts:2:15: warning eslint(no-use-before-define): 'Child' was used before it was defined.
```

Both ESLint 9.39.4 (`no-use-before-define`) and typescript-eslint 8.60.1 (`@typescript-eslint/no-use-before-define`) produce no diagnostics for this same TypeScript source with the options above. I verified both using ESLint's Linter API and `@typescript-eslint/parser`.

### Expected behavior

Match ESLint/typescript-eslint by accepting this instance field initializer with `classes: false`. The initializer runs when `Parent` is instantiated, rather than when its class declaration is evaluated. This report concerns non-static instance fields; static initialization has different evaluation timing.

ESLint documents `classes: false` as allowing references to declarations in upper function scopes: https://eslint.org/docs/latest/rules/no-use-before-define#classes

Related parity issue: #19504, which reports a different case (a missing diagnostic inside a function).

issue.title: feat(linter): add debug-allocs feature for profiling rule memory
issue.body:
This is a new CLI debugging feature that should help to identify rules that allocate a lot of memory (not necessarily correlating with peak resident set size though). It can be enabled with `--debug memory`, similar to `--debug timings`. 

I chose to put this behind the `debug_allocs` Cargo feature though because I couldn't think of a way to ensure this had no overhead if not using the debug flag, because we have to install a custom global allocator that tracks the number of allocations. This makes it a lower risk addition to the CLI, but at the cost of requiring you to manually compile it, so it's not available for end-users by default like `--debug timings` is. I think that's a fair tradeoff to make though since it'll still make it easy to identify rules doing lots of allocations.

The goal of this new feature is to give a quantifiable and deterministic metric that can be used to optimize the amount of memory used by a lint rule. This means that it is easier to verify that lint rule changes actually have a performance benefit since right now we don't have an easy way to verify memory improvements.

issue.title: linter: jsx-a11y/aria-role reports role={undefined}, which eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y allows
issue.body:
### What version of Oxlint are you using?

1.90.0

### What command did you run?

oxlint repro.tsx

### What does your `.oxlintrc.json` (or `oxlint.config.ts`) config file look like?

```jsonc
{
  "categories": { "correctness": "off" },
  "plugins": ["jsx-a11y"],
  "rules": { "jsx-a11y/aria-role": "error" }
}
```

### What happened?

`role={undefined}` is reported as an invalid role:

```tsx
declare const Button: (props: { role?: string }) => null;

export const A = () => <Button role={undefined} />;
export const B = () => <div role={undefined} />;
```

```
repro.tsx:3:32: error jsx-a11y(aria-role): Elements with ARIA roles must use a valid, non-abstract ARIA role.
repro.tsx:4:29: error jsx-a11y(aria-role): Elements with ARIA roles must use a valid, non-abstract ARIA role.
```

eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y 6.10.2 (ESLint 9.39.5) reports nothing. Its rule skips
`undefined` on purpose:

```js
// If value is undefined, then the role attribute will be dropped in the DOM.
if (value === undefined || value === null) {
  return;
}
```

In `aria_role.rs`, `jsexp.is_undefined()` sits next to the `NullLiteral` check
and both report. `role={null}` is a fail case upstream too, so null is fine,
but no Oxlint test covers `undefined`.

We hit this with MUI: passing `role={undefined}` is how you remove a role MUI

issue.title: linter: no-use-before-define flags instance fields with classes: false
issue.body:
### What version of Oxlint are you using?

1.90.0

### What command did you run?

```sh
oxlint --config .oxlintrc.json --max-warnings 0 example.ts
```

### What does your `.oxlintrc.json` config file look like?

```json
{
  "rules": {
    "no-use-before-define": [
      "warn",
      { "functions": false, "classes": false, "variables": false }
    ]
  }
}
```

### Minimal reproduction

```ts
export class Parent {
  child = new Child();
}

class Child {}
```

### What happened?

Oxlint reports the reference in the instance field initializer:

```text
example.ts:2:15: warning eslint(no-use-before-define): 'Child' was used before it was defined.
```

Both ESLint 9.39.4 (`no-use-before-define`) and typescript-eslint 8.60.1 (`@typescript-eslint/no-use-before-define`) produce no diagnostics for this same TypeScript source with the options above. I verified both using ESLint's Linter API and `@typescript-eslint/parser`.

### Expected behavior

Match ESLint/typescript-eslint by accepting this instance field initializer with `classes: false`. The initializer runs when `Parent` is instantiated, rather than when its class declaration is evaluated. This report concerns non-static instance fields; static initialization has different evaluation timing.

ESLint documents `classes: false` as allowing references to declarations in upper function scopes: https://eslint.org/docs/latest/rules/no-use-before-define#classes

Related parity issue: #19504, which reports a different case (a missing diagnostic inside a function).

issue.title: fix(linter/no-restricted-imports): respect allowTypeImports for `import type {}`
issue.body:
`import type {} from '...'` has no specifiers, so it never produces an import entry and the rule handled it in the side-effect path. That path ignored `allowTypeImports`, so the statement got reported even though it is a type import. This is the pattern MUI X documents for loading its theme augmentation, so it shows up a lot.

The side-effect map now records whether each statement was `import type` (from `RequestedModule::is_type`), and paths/patterns with `allowTypeImports: true` skip those statements. Plain `import {} from '...'` is still reported.

## Testing

- Added pass cases for `import type {}` with a pattern and a path that set `allowTypeImports`, and fail cases for the same thing without `type`.
- `cargo test -p oxc_linter --lib no_restricted_imports` fails without the fix and passes with it.
- `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy -p oxc_linter -- -D warnings`

AI disclosure: I used Claude Code while working on this. I reviewed the change and ran the tests myself.

Closes #28780

issue.title: semantic: sloppy TypeScript scripts disagree with the post-transform checker on block function bindings
issue.body:
## Summary

The TypeScript binder has no Annex B: a function declaration in a block of a sloppy-mode TypeScript script stays bound in its block. The TypeScript transform switches the program's `source_type` to JavaScript (`crates/oxc_transformer/src/typescript/mod.rs`, `enter_program`), and `check_semantic_after_transform` rebuilds semantic data from that program as JavaScript, which does apply Annex B hoisting. The transformed `Scoping` and the rebuilt one therefore disagree for block functions in sloppy TypeScript scripts, e.g. `.cts` files.

## Reproduction (`main` @ 4c47b4d330)

Add `tasks/coverage/misc/pass/block-fn.cts`:

```ts
{ function f() {} }
f();
```

Then run `cargo coverage semantic --filter block-fn`:

```
Bindings mismatch:
after transform: ScopeId(0): []
rebuilt        : ScopeId(0): ["f"]
Bindings mismatch:
after transform: ScopeId(1): ["f"]
rebuilt        : ScopeId(1): []
Symbol scope ID mismatch for "f":
...
Unresolved references mismatch:
after transform: ["f"]
rebuilt        : []
```

`function t() { { function g() {} } return g; }` fails the same way.

## Notes

- After #28765 and its stacked follow-up (function declarations in `if` branches get their own scope), `if (c) function f() {} else function f() {}` in a sloppy TypeScript script joins this class. The single-branch case still matches, because the TypeScript binder binds an `if`-branch function in the scope enclosing the `if`.
- Options: model Annex B for sloppy TypeScript the way `tsc` does (it binds sloppy-mode block functions in the container), or reconcile the bindings when the transform switches to JavaScript.

This issue was drafted with AI assistance (Cursor agent). I reproduced it locally.

issue.title: feat(linter): support inline /* global */ declarations and disabling globals with off
issue.body:
## Feature request

Support ESLint-style `/* global */` comments as per-file additions to, or removals from, the globals known to Oxlint's native rules, including `no-undef`.

I understand that these comments are currently unsupported: #18308 skips conformance tests that depend on them, and the open #28577 adds a diagnostic for unsupported directives. This is a request to add compatibility, rather than a regression report. That diagnostic would help users discover the limitation, but would not provide the requested behavior.

## Motivation

In our project, some Node.js scripts use Playwright to evaluate callbacks in the browser. We use a file-local `/* global document */` declaration for those scripts, while keeping the surrounding Node.js environment. We also need to retain the ability to remove an environment-provided global from an individual file with `off`.

We currently keep `no-undef` in ESLint because moving it to Oxlint changes the results for both cases below. Supporting these declarations would let us move this check to Oxlint while retaining the existing source-level declarations. We would still use ESLint for other checks.

## Minimal reproduction

Tested with Oxlint **1.91.0**, ESLint **10.14.0**, and Node.js **26.13.0** on macOS arm64, in an isolated directory outside the project configuration.

`oxlint.json`:

```json
{
  "env": {
    "node": true,
    "browser": false
  }
}
```

Only `no-undef` is enabled by the commands below.

### 1. Declare a global for one file

`declare.mjs`:

```js
/* global document */
document.createElement("div");
```

```sh
oxlint -c oxlint.json -A all -D no-undef --format unix declare.mjs
```

Actual result: exit code **1**:

```text
declare.mjs:2:1: 'document' is not defined. [Error/eslint(no-undef)]
```

Requested result: accept `document` in this file, as ESLint does.

### 2. Remove an environment-provided global for one file

`remove.mjs`:

```js
/* global process: off */
process.cwd();
```

```sh
oxlint -c oxlint.json -A all -D no-undef --format unix remove.mjs
```

Actual result: exit code **0**, with no diagnostics.

Requested result: report `'process' is not defined.` because the file-local `off` declaration overrides the global enabled by `env.node`.

### ESLint comparison

The corresponding ESLint flat configuration, with only the relevant Node global enabled, is:

```js
export default [
  {
    languageOptions: {
      globals: { process: "readonly" }
    },
    rules: { "no-undef": "error" }
  }
];
```

With that configuration, ESLint reports no errors for `declare.mjs` and one `no-undef` error for `remove.mjs`. As controls, removing the comments causes both tools to report the undeclared `document` and accept `process`.

## Requested behavior

- Honor file-local global declarations, including the shorthand above and explicit `readonly` / `writable` modes, following [ESLint's global-comment semantics](https://eslint.org/docs/latest/use/configure/language-options#use-configuration-comments).
- Honor `off` for a name enabled by the environment or configuration.
- Keep these changes local to the file; an undeclared identifier in another file should still be reported.

An opt-in compatibility setting would also address our use case. This request concerns global declarations only; it does not require changing rule-suppression semantics or supporting arbitrary inline rule configuration.

AI assistance: I used Codex to investigate the behavior, run the reproduction and control cases, check related issues, and draft this report.

issue.title: fix(linter/unicorn/require-post-message-target-origin): ignore BroadcastChannel and Worker instances
issue.body:
`unicorn/require-post-message-target-origin` no longer reports `postMessage()` calls on `BroadcastChannel` and `Worker` instances. Their `postMessage()` methods take no `targetOrigin` argument, and the rule's suggestion inserted `channel.location.origin` / `worker.location.origin`, properties those objects don't have.

Closes #28596

The rule now skips a call when its receiver is a `new BroadcastChannel(...)` or `new Worker(...)` expression, or an identifier bound to a `const` initialized with one (parentheses and TS `as`/`satisfies`/`!` are looked through). This extends the existing message-port heuristic and follows the `const`-initializer check that `unicorn/prefer-at` uses for receivers. The constructor is matched by name, so `Worker` imported from `node:worker_threads` is covered too. `let`/`var` bindings are not trusted because they can be reassigned to a window. The rule docs now describe which receivers are ignored.

`window.postMessage(message)` is still reported, as the issue asks. `self.postMessage(message)` is also still reported: in a dedicated worker it is `DedicatedWorkerGlobalScope#postMessage()`, but without type information it cannot be told apart from `self` in a window, where the report and the `self.location.origin` suggestion are correct. Upstream eslint-plugin-unicorn now uses type information for this; the native rule only has local evidence.

Validation:

- `cargo test --all-features -p oxc_linter` (`just test -p oxc_linter`): passed; lib 1287 passed, 1 ignored; all integration test binaries and doc-tests passed.
- The 8 new pass cases (constructor-bound `const`s, in-place `new`, optional call, TS `as`, a `node:worker_threads` import, a closure) fail without the fix: with the new check removed, the rule test reports `8 test cases expected to pass, but failed`, exactly those cases.
- New fail cases keep reporting: a `const` bound to `window.open(url)`, a reassigned `let`, a parameter shadowing a `const` worker, and `new Foo().postMessage(message)`. The snapshot adds only these four diagnostics.
- `CARGO_BUILD_WARNINGS=deny cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features -p oxc_linter` (`just lint -p oxc_linter`): passed.
- `rustfmt --check` on the changed file: passed. `cargo lintgen`: no changes to generated files.
- `typos` is not installed locally, so the typo check was left to CI.

new rule - enforce variance keywords on generics in typescript

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

issue.body:
i've just switched to oxlint from eslint and i'm very happy with how much easier it is to configure. the only thing missing (aside from not-yet-implemented rules that already have open issues) is a rule i created for my eslint plugin, [`require-variance-annotations`](https://github.com/DetachHead/eslint-plugin-detachhead/blob/master/docs/rules/require-variance-annotations.md)

i can't use my plugin with oxlint unfortunately because i could never get it to work with the new eslint 9+ config format. i would consider trying to recreate this plugin for oxlint, but was wondering if it was something that would be accepted into oxlint itself.

the motivation for this rule is outlined in its docs:

> typescript infers the variance of generics based on their usage, but there are several benefits to defining the variance explicitly:
> 
> -   it can be a useful for a reader to explicitly see how a type parameter is used at a glance
> -   can increase performance as the typescript compiler does not need to perform expensive checks to infer the variance where it's explicitly defined
> -   can prevent unintentional breaking changes in your API if, for example, a new method is added to a class that changes the variance of its generic

comment.body:
> > The TS docs have quite a few caveats on variance annotations, which I agree with. (https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/generics.html#variance-annotations). It's not a feature that should be generally used.
>         
>         
> Which caveats exactly? Those docs seem to insist that you should _only_ use them when absolutely necessary but doesnt really explain why. In other languages like Python and Kotlin, specifying the variance explicitly is the norm. I think it's something people should do more often for the reasons I mentioned above

I'm not saying variance annotations aren't useful, I just don't think we should support a new rule in `oxc` for this right now. As the docs say, you should very rarely need this because the compiler can infer it nearly all of the time. If it's something that more codebases would benefit from though, then I think developing a custom plugin to enforce it would be a great first step.

i've just switched to oxlint from eslint and i'm very happy with how much easier it is to configure. the only thing missing (aside from not-yet-implemented rules that already have open issues) is a rule i created for my eslint plugin, [`require-variance-annotations`](https://github.com/DetachHead/eslint-plugin-detachhead/blob/master/docs/rules/require-variance-annotations.md)

issue.title: Support JSON output for `--debug timings`

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

issue.body:
## Description

`oxlint --format json` currently outputs diagnostics and execution summary information, but it does not include data collected by `--debug timings`.

Please expose timing data as structured JSON when both options are enabled:

```sh
oxlint --debug timings --format json
```

This would allow downstream tools, such as [oxc-devtools](https://devtools.vite.dev/oxc/), to consume timing data reliably and provide richer visualizations.

## Proposed output
Add a rule_timings field to the existing top-level JSON object only when --debug timings is enabled:

```json
{
  "diagnostics": [],
  "number_of_files": 1,
  "number_of_rules": 42,
  "threads_count": 1,
  "start_time": 0.01,
  "rule_timings": {
    "records": [
      {
        "source": "native",
        "plugin_name": "eslint",
        "rule_name": "no-debugger",
        "duration_ms": 1.5,
        "calls": 3
      }
    ],
    "js_plugin_runtime_ms": 0
  }
}
```

comment.body: I think it would make sense for this to work with the JSON formatter for automated tooling case. I don't think we should put a lot of work into making it work with other formatters though. I'll look into it.
